opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think multimodal learning is exciting because robots, unlike chatbots, have to deal with the physical world, and the physical world doesn't come to you in a single stream. A person picking up a coffee mug is using vision, but also touch, proprioception, a sense of weight, even sound sometimes. When you hear the mug scrape on the table, that tells you something about friction. For a long time in robotics we tried to do almost everything from vision alone, or from carefully engineered models of geometry and physics. What we're seeing now is that if you can combine these signals, say camera images with tactile sensing and force feedback, and increasingly with language, the system can become much more robust.

Language is an interesting piece of this. It gives us a way to specify tasks that's very natural. You can say "fold the towel" or "clear the table" rather than programming waypoints. And these large vision-language models carry a lot of common-sense knowledge about objects: that a mug has a handle, that a glass is fragile. That's genuinely useful as a prior.

But I want to be careful here, because there's a lot of hype. I often talk about what I call the "data gap." Language models were trained on something like the equivalent of tens of thousands of years of human reading. In robotics we have nothing close to that amount of data for physical interaction. So multimodal learning is exciting partly because it lets us borrow from the modalities where we do have lots of data, images and text, and connect that to the much scarcer data about actually manipulating things.

I'm also a believer that we shouldn't throw away good old-fashioned engineering. Physics, geometry, control theory. These still matter. The most promising path, I think, is combining learned multimodal models with those classical methods, and then collecting data as robots are deployed, so they improve over time. That's what makes it exciting to me. It's not that we've solved it, it's that we can finally see a plausible route toward robots that can handle the messiness of real homes and warehouses.

r001.rationale: The response says combining sensory signals can make robots more robust, but does not explain that training on simultaneously observed modalities teaches relationships between them.

r002.rationale: The response does not say a network can infer information from a missing modality using the remaining modalities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've been working on robot grasping and manipulation for a long time, and for most of that history we treated each sensing modality in isolation. You'd have a vision pipeline, maybe a separate force or tactile pipeline, and then some hand-engineered logic trying to stitch them together. It was brittle. The robot would see a cup, compute a grasp, and then have no graceful way to recover when the cup turned out to be slippery or heavier than expected.

What excites me about multimodal learning is that it mirrors how humans actually do this. When you reach into a bag to find your keys, you're not relying on vision at all. When you pour coffee, you're using sight, the feel of the weight shifting, maybe even the sound. These channels are redundant and complementary, and the brain fuses them seamlessly. Now we're starting to see learned models that can do something similar, taking in images, depth, touch, proprioception, and language all at once, and finding correlations across them that a human engineer would never think to write down.

The language piece is particularly interesting to me. For decades, if you wanted a robot to do a new task, you essentially had to reprogram it. The idea that you could say "move the red mug away from the edge of the table" and have the system ground that in what it sees and feels, that's a real shift. It opens up robots to people who aren't roboticists.

Now, I want to be a bit careful here, because I'm a known skeptic about some of the hype. Multimodal models still struggle with the physics. They can describe a scene beautifully and then fail to pick up a crumpled towel. Data is the bottleneck. Internet-scale text and images exist; internet-scale tactile data does not. So I think of multimodal learning as a very promising direction that is going to need a lot of careful work on the data side, on simulation, and on combining learning with good old-fashioned models of contact and friction. But the fact that we can even frame the problem this way now is genuinely exciting to me.

r001.rationale: It says learned models take images, depth, touch, proprioception, and language together and find correlations across them, which communicates learning relationships between simultaneously observed modalities.

r002.rationale: The response describes humans using some senses without vision, but does not say that a multimodal network can use available modalities to infer information from a missing one.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that robots have to connect what they perceive with what they do. Vision is tremendously useful, but it doesn’t tell you everything. If you’re grasping an object, you also want to know: Have I made contact? Is it slipping? How much force am I applying? Touch and force sensing give you information that an image alone can’t provide.

And those signals can help interpret one another. Imagine looking at a piece of fabric. It can be difficult to tell where one layer ends and another begins. But if you pinch it and lift it a little, you get new visual information and tactile information. You’re taking an action to resolve uncertainty.

That’s a very exciting direction: learning across those different sources of information, and connecting them to actions. There are still hard questions about how much data we need and how well these systems generalize. But the possibility is that a robot can become much better at dealing with the ambiguity of the physical world.

r002.rationale: It says touch and force provide information beyond images, but does not explain that a network can infer information from a missing modality using the remaining modalities.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is that a robot has to connect what it sees with what it does and what it feels. Vision alone can be ambiguous. You might see an object and have a good guess about its shape, but you don’t know how heavy it is, whether it’s slippery, or whether it will deform when you grasp it. Touch and motion give you information that an image can’t.

And those signals can help teach one another. If the robot reaches for something and it slips, that experience can improve its understanding of what it was seeing. Language adds another way to communicate what we want the robot to accomplish.

The exciting possibility is that combining these sources of information will help robots handle unfamiliar situations. That’s a central challenge in robotics: getting a system to work reliably when the objects and conditions aren’t exactly the ones it encountered during training.

r001.rationale: The response says vision, touch, and motion can inform one another, including that a slip experience can improve the robot’s understanding of what it saw. This communicates learning relationships between modalities.

r002.rationale: It says touch and motion provide information an image cannot, but does not explain that a network can infer information from a modality that is missing.
